topic: The Dunning-Kruger effect: what it really says
title: Dunning-Kruger: What Everyone Gets Wrong
voiceover: Do unskilled people really think they're geniuses? In 1999, Justin Kruger and David Dunning tested people on humor, grammar and logic. Those who scored in the bottom quarter guessed they'd done much better than they had. They scored around the 12th percentile but estimated themselves near the 62nd. The researchers argued that skill and the ability to judge your skill are linked. When they trained participants, those participants became better at recognizing their own limits. But here's the catch: a 2020 study of 929 people argued that the classic pattern is mostly a statistical artifact. It found that self-rated and measured intelligence rose together in almost a straight line. So when you're learning something new, building skill may also improve your ability to judge your own work. Tomorrow: why is that song stuck in your head?

description: Do unskilled people really think they're geniuses? Not quite: in the original study the lowest scorers overestimated their rank, but a 2020 analysis argued much of the classic pattern is a statistical artefact. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Kruger, J., & Dunning, D. (1999). Unskilled and unaware of it: How difficulties in recognizing one's own incompetence lead to inflated self-assessments. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 77(6), 1121-1134. Source: Gignac, G. E., & Zajenkowski, M. (2020). The Dunning-Kruger effect is (mostly) a statistical artefact: Valid approaches to testing the hypothesis with individual differences data. Intelligence, 80, 101449.
accuracy_note: CONTESTED. Gignac & Zajenkowski (2020) used intelligence tests in 929 community participants; their critique applies to that way of testing, and Dunning and others dispute it. The popular 'Mount Stupid' graph is not from the 1999 paper (not used here).
